heading: Did you know?
foundry_updates: Use Check for updates in Foundry Settings to see if a new release is available.
foundry_history: Open History to find saved runs and return to a previous result.
foundry_rocket: Rocket Mode runs the remaining stages and prepares your selected exports.
foundry_connect: Use Connect your agent to get setup instructions for Codex, Claude Code, or another MCP client.
foundry_agent: Your agent can check a Foundry job through MCP while it works on other parts of your project.
foundry_models: In Settings, sort installed models by name, size, or date added to find what you need.
foundry_unload: Unload models when you’re finished to free memory for your next task.
foundry_font: Use the Font menu to make wizard controls and previews easier to read.
foundry_gallery: Save a generated image to the Gallery so you can reuse it in another workflow.
foundry_package: The export ZIP includes a README that describes the files and lists applicable notices.
pinokio_setup: Pinokio sets up Foundry’s software dependencies in its own installation.
pinokio_update: To update a Pinokio installation, use Update in the Foundry app’s sidebar.
pinokio_listing: The Pinokio website shows what’s available. Pinokio Desktop manages the copy on your PC.
pinokio_first_use: Foundry usually downloads model weights on first use. Later runs can reuse the downloaded files.
pinokio_logs: If startup fails in Pinokio, open Startup logs to see which step needs attention.
pinokio_repair: Pinokio’s Repair software reruns Foundry’s setup and keeps your saved assets and models.
pinokio_restart: After stopping Foundry in Pinokio, use Start Foundry and then Open Foundry to return.
pinokio_install_url: You can install Foundry in Pinokio Desktop by pasting its GitHub repository URL.
pinokio_community: If you share a workflow in the Pinokio community, include an example result and the hardware you used.
pinokio_reload: After updating, reload any already-open Foundry page to pick up the new interface.
pinokio_dev_install: Give people a one-click way to try your project. A Pinokio launcher can turn your setup commands into an Install button and give users a Start button to get running.
pinokio_dev_gepeto: Build the launcher with your coding agent. Pinokio’s Gepeto skill gives your agent a starting point for turning a GitHub project into a shareable Pinokio app.
pinokio_dev_live_logs: See what your app is doing while you build it. Pinokio lets you run the app beside its live server logs, so you can see what happened as soon as you try a feature.
pinokio_dev_pterm: Give your coding agent a way to test the app it just built. With Pinokio’s pterm command, the agent can launch the app, check whether it’s ready, and read its logs.
pinokio_dev_bug_reports: Make bug reports easier to act on. Pinokio can gather the logs from a specific run into a report you can review and share with the community or bring to your coding agent.
reference_three_quarter: A three-quarter reference can show both the front and the depth of a prop.
reference_background: Choose a plain background with good contrast around the subject.
reference_crop: Leave a little space around the subject so the reference shows its whole outline.
reference_lighting: Even lighting helps keep hard shadows from reading as part of the object.
images_material: Describe the surface as well as the shape. Weathered wood and polished steel read very differently.
images_reverse: If a rear detail matters, describe it when making a front and back pair.
images_seed: Keep the same seed when comparing changes to a prompt or one setting.
images_variation: Use a new variation to explore a different image from the same idea.
orbit_single_turn: For reconstruction, ask for one smooth 360° orbit at a steady speed.
orbit_stationary: Keep the subject still during the orbit. Let the camera do the moving.
orbit_blur: If you can choose frames, favor sharp views where thin parts are easy to see.
orbit_inspect: Watch the whole orbit before reconstruction. Check that it completes the turn and keeps the same shape.
views_consistency: Use views that agree on the subject’s shape and proportions.
views_details: Keep one-sided details on the same side in every view.
views_label: Check the view labels before building the mesh, especially the front and back.
views_coverage: Pick angles that reveal different parts of the object and still overlap with neighboring views.
geometry_silhouette: Check the outline of the untextured mesh before judging materials.
geometry_unseen: A part hidden in every reference has to be inferred. Add a view if that part matters.
geometry_refiner: Compare the refined mesh with the initial mesh to see what changed around thin parts.
geometry_quads: Quad retopology can make editing easier. Review how the edges flow around joints before rigging.
texture_resolution: Larger texture maps use more memory. Inspect the asset at its intended size before increasing resolution.
texture_back: Check the back and underside of the textured asset before export.
texture_maps: Review the color map and normal map separately when a surface looks wrong.
texture_light: Even reference lighting helps keep highlights and shadows out of the baked color.
splat_pair: A Gaussian splat captures appearance. Its companion mesh gives you geometry to edit.
splat_brush: Orbit with Splats sets up Brush automatically the first time you train a splat.
splat_budget: Use a smaller splat preset for a quick check and compare before increasing the budget.
splat_collision: Use the companion mesh as a starting point for collision and check its fit in your engine.
ccore_single_prop: Give CCORE one prop at a time and describe the parts that distinguish it.
ccore_examples: Load a CCORE example to see how shape, materials, and details fit into one description.
ccore_budget: A larger CCORE generation budget uses more GPU memory. Start with a budget that fits your card.
ccore_image: With a CCORE image reference, say which details to keep and what you want to change.
hair_visible: For HairDeck, choose an image where the hairstyle’s outer shape is easy to see.
hair_variation: Compare HairDeck variations from the side and back before choosing one to export.
garment_drape: Review the garment drape and sewing pattern before fitting it to a character.
garment_pose: Check for clipping in the poses you intend to use after fitting a garment.
export_glb: GLB is a convenient way to bring a textured mesh into Blender.
export_stl: Before printing an STL, check the size and inspect the model in your slicer.
export_scale: Check the scale and orientation after importing your asset into Blender or a game engine.
export_compact: Preview the compact mesh at game distance to see which details still read.
